llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – “AIR‐FREIGHT–INDUCED TRADE AND NATIONAL INCOME, 1960-1995”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–stage least squares (IV) embedded in a difference-in-differences framework.

Rationale  
•  Endogeneity of trade: richer (or faster-growing) countries both trade more and earn more.  
•  The post-1955 fall in air‐freight costs is a technology shock that is (i) global, (ii) unrelated to any single country’s growth path, and (iii) interacts mechanically with geography.  
•  Geography is time-invariant; only its interaction with the exogenous fall in air costs varies over time.  
•  We first show that country-level trade openness rose more for nations whose trade partners lie “far by sea but near by air.” We then use that predicted, technology-driven change in trade to instrument the actual change in trade when estimating its effect on income.

Formally  
Stage 1 (gravity-based first stage):  
Δln Trade_ct = α_c + γ_t + β · AirAdvantage_c × Post_t + ε_ct

Stage 2:  
Δln GDPpc_ct = α_c + γ_t + θ · Ĥln Trade_ct + u_ct  

where Ĥln Trade_ct is the fitted value from stage 1. Fixed effects absorb all time-invariant country characteristics and global shocks common to everybody; the interaction term provides the quasi-experimental variation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (continuous): ln Trade openness = ln[(Exports+Imports)/GDP].

Instrument (“dose” of treatment):  
AirAdvantage_c = Σ_p s_cp · [(SeaDist_cp – GCircDist_cp)/SeaDist_cp]  
 • s_cp = share of partner p in country c’s total trade in the base year 1960  
 • Larger values mean “much farther by sea than by air.”

Treatment timing: technology shock starts in the late 1950s; we treat 1960 as pre-treatment and allow a flexible post-trend (e.g., linear or piecewise spline starting 1965).

Control group: countries in the lowest quartile of AirAdvantage_c (their sea and air distances are roughly the same, so they benefited little from aviation).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: AirAdvantage_c × Post_t must predict changes in trade.  
 • Plausible: compositional U.S. data show air’s share rose fastest on long-by-sea routes; we will verify a strong F-statistic (>10).

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on country and year fixed effects, AirAdvantage_c affects GDP only through trade.  
 • Plausible: geography is predetermined, and aviation technology is external to an individual country’s policies.  
 • Remaining concern: Air traffic might facilitate FDI, tourism, or knowledge diffusion independently of goods trade (addressed in Section 4).

A3. No differential pre-trends (parallel trends) between high- and low-advantage countries before 1960.  
 • Testable via event-study coefficients for 1950-1960.

A4. Stable unit treatment value: one country’s treatment intensity does not directly shift another’s income beyond normal general-equilibrium effects that are part of “trade.”  
 • Reasonable at the country level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Other contemporaneous innovations (containerization, telecom) correlated with AirAdvantage_c.  
 • Add control interactions: (i) PortContainer_c × Post_t, (ii) SubmarineCable_c × Post_t.  
 • Restrict sample to non-containerizable goods (using HS categories) as a robustness check.

T2. AirAdvantage_c correlated with unobserved geography that drives growth (e.g., land size, remoteness).  
 • Country fixed effects wipe out level differences; we additionally control for Time-Varying Remoteness = average great-circle distance to all partners interacted with year dummies.  
 • Placebo test: replicate first and second stages back to 1940-1955—coefficients should be zero.

T3. Direct effect of aviation via tourism, migration, or air-mail.  
 • Control for international tourism arrivals per capita (UNWTO) where available.  
 • Exclude service-economy-dependent small islands (Bahamas, Seychelles) and re-estimate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast FELM + IV
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# --- 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------
trade   <- fread("bilateral_trade_1950_1997.csv")   # i,j,t,trade_value
dist    <- fread("pair_distance.csv")               # i,j,SeaDist,GCircDist
gdp     <- fread("gdp_pc_1960_1995.csv")            # i,t,GDPpc
controls<- fread("country_controls.csv")            # tourism, container ports

# --- 2. Construct Air Advantage ----------------------------------
# compute baseline 1960 partner shares
trade_1960 <- trade[year==1960]
trade_1960[, share := trade_value / sum(trade_value), by=i]

# merge distances
trade_1960 <- merge(trade_1960, dist, by=c("i","j"))

trade_1960[, adv_ij := (SeaDist - GCircDist)/SeaDist]
adv_country <- trade_1960[, .(AirAdvantage = sum(share * adv_ij)), by=i]

# --- 3. Collapse trade to country-year ---------------------------
trade_ct <- trade[, .(Trade = sum(trade_value)), by=.(i, year)]
gdp[, lnGDPpc := log(GDPpc)]
trade_ct[, lnTrade := log(Trade)]

# merge AirAdvantage and GDP
panel <- merge(trade_ct, adv_country, by="i", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, gdp[,.(i, year, lnGDPpc)], by=c("i","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, controls, by=c("i","year"), all.x=TRUE)

# define post indicator & instrument
panel[, Post := ifelse(year >= 1965, 1, 0)]
panel[, Z := AirAdvantage * Post]

# --- 4. Main 2SLS specification ----------------------------------
fe_iv <- feols(lnGDPpc ~ 1 | lnTrade ~ Z,      # 2SLS
               data = panel,
               fixef = c("i","year"),
               cluster = "i")                  # cluster by country
summary(fe_iv, se = "cluster")

# --- 5. Robustness: placebo pre-trend ----------------------------
panel[, PrePlacebo := ifelse(year %in% 1950:1955, 1, 0)]
panel[, Z_placebo := AirAdvantage * PrePlacebo]

fe_iv_placebo <- feols(lnGDPpc ~ 1 | lnTrade ~ Z_placebo,
                       data = panel[year <= 1965],
                       fixef = c("i","year"),
                       cluster = "i")
summary(fe_iv_placebo, se = "cluster")
```

Notes:  
• Data must be reshaped so that country code “i” = ISO3.  
• fixest automatically does the two stages and reports first-stage F.  
• Additional robustness: drop tourism-intensive island economies (`panel[!isIsland]`).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: positive — greater trade openness raises income per capita.

Magnitude (prior): Guided by macro theory with σ = 1.5–2.0 and prior estimates (Frankel & Romer 1999; Feyrer 2019), I expect θ ≈ 0.5. Thus a 10 percent increase in trade/GDP would raise real GDP per capita by roughly 5 percent over the long run.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV-DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Relevance (first-stage F > 10) ......................................... 1  
C2: Independence / as-good-as random variation ............................. 0.5  
C3: Exclusion (no direct aviation effect on income) ........................ 0.5  
C4: No differential pre-trends (tested via event study) .................... 1  
C5: Correct functional form & standard errors (FE, clustering) ............. 1  

Total ≈ 4/5. Remaining unease lies in potential direct aviation channels, which robustness checks attempt to rule out.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan exploits a plausibly exogenous, geography-based change in effective bilateral distances caused by the advent of air freight to isolate the causal impact of trade on national income.
